title: Call Stack & Synchronous Execution
concept: JavaScript is a single-threaded language that manages function execution through the call stack

steps.title: Calling first()
steps.explanation:
When first() is called, it gets pushed onto the **call stack**.

The call stack is a data structure that tracks currently executing functions. It follows LIFO (Last In First Out) - the most recently added function executes first.

**Why Single Thread?**
JavaScript was designed for the browser where:
- DOM manipulation must be consistent (no race conditions)
- Simple mental model for developers
- Memory efficiency (no thread overhead)

steps.title: Executing console.log('first')
steps.explanation:
We enter the first() function body.

console.log gets pushed to the call stack, executes immediately to print 'first', then gets popped off the stack.

steps.title: Calling second()
steps.explanation:
The second() function is called.

While first() hasn't finished yet, second() gets pushed on top of the stack. This is the core concept of the **function call stack**.

steps.title: Executing console.log('second')
steps.explanation:
Inside second(), console.log executes.

'second' is printed, and console.log is popped from the stack.

steps.title: second() completes
steps.explanation:
second() finishes and is popped from the call stack.

Execution returns to first(). The top of the stack is now first() again.

steps.title: Executing console.log('first end')
steps.explanation:
The remaining code in first() executes.

'first end' is printed.

steps.title: first() completes
steps.explanation:
first() finishes completely and is popped from the call stack.

**Stack Overflow Warning**
If a function calls itself infinitely:
```
function infinite() { infinite(); }
```
The stack keeps growing until it exceeds the limit (typically 10,000-50,000 frames), causing a **Stack Overflow** error.

steps.title: Executing console.log('done')
steps.explanation:
Back to global code, the final console.log executes.

**Execution order**: first -> second -> first end -> done

Synchronous code runs sequentially, and function calls stack up LIFO style.

**But wait...** If JavaScript is single-threaded, how does it handle timers and network requests without freezing? That's what we'll learn in the next lesson!

quiz.explanation: Function calls are pushed onto the call stack. a() executes printing 1 -> b() is called printing 2 -> b() returns, a() continues printing 3

misconceptions.wrong: JavaScript can execute multiple functions at the same time
misconceptions.correct: JavaScript is single-threaded. Only one function can execute at a time.
misconceptions.why: Only the function at the top of the call stack is executing.

misconceptions.correct: Infinite recursion causes a Stack Overflow error when the call stack limit is exceeded.
misconceptions.why: Each function call adds a frame to the stack. Browser engines have a limit (typically 10,000-50,000 frames) to prevent memory exhaustion.

misconceptions.wrong: Single-threaded means JavaScript can only do one thing ever
misconceptions.correct: Single-threaded means one thing at a time on the main thread, but async operations can run in parallel via Web APIs.
misconceptions.why: The Event Loop (next lesson) enables concurrency without multi-threading.

keyTakeaway: Call Stack = Tracks executing functions, LIFO order. Single thread = one thing at a time (but async helps!)
